$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{9k-5}{6} & =\frac{k}{2} \\ (9k-5)\cdot 2 & =6\cdot k\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we proceed as usual to solve the equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}(9k-5)\cdot 2 & =6\cdot k \\ 18k-10 & =6k \\ 18k-10-18k & =6k-18k \\ -10 & =-12k \\ \frac{-10}{-12} & =\frac{-12k}{-12} \\ \frac{10}{12} & =k \\ \frac{5}{6} & =k\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, $k=\frac{5}{6}.$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{2x+5}{30} & =\frac{1}{2} \\ (2x+5)\cdot 2 & =30\cdot 1\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we proceed as usual to solve the equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}(2x+5)\cdot 2 & =30\cdot 1 \\ 4x+10 & =30 \\ 4x+10-10 & =30-10 \\ 4x & =20 \\ \frac{4x}{4} & =\frac{20}{4} \\ x & =5\end{aligned}
$$

$$

$$

Then, we proceed as usual to solve the equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}(u+2)\cdot 2 & =3\cdot (-3+u) \\ 2u+4 & =-9+3u \\ 2u+4-2u & =-9+3u-2u \\ 4 & =-9+u \\ 4+9 & =-9+u+9 \\ 13 & =u\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $u=13.$

tutorials.name: Introduction
tutorials.problem:
If we have rational expressions on both sides of an equation, say,

$$
\dfrac{{\color{red}x-1}}{{\color{blue}2}} = \dfrac{{\color{blue}2x-1}}{{\color{red}5}},
$$

then we can eliminate the rational expressions by applying **cross-multiplication**:

- we cross-multiply the left-hand side numerator $({\color{red}x-1})$ with the right-hand side denominator $({\color{red}5}),$ and

- we cross-multiply the left-hand side denominator $({\color{blue}2})$ with the right-hand side numerator $({\color{blue}2x-1}).$

Doing this, we get the following equation:

$$
({\color{red}x-1}) \cdot ({\color{red}5}) = ({\color{blue}2}) \cdot ({\color{blue}2x - 1})
$$

After we've cross-multiplied, we proceed as usual to solve the equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}(x-1)\cdot 5 & =2\cdot (2x-1) \\ 5x-5 & =4x-2 \\ 5x-5+5 & =4x-2+5 \\ 5x & =4x+3 \\ 5x-4x & =4x+3-4x \\ x & =3\end{aligned}
$$

**Note:** Cross-multiplication might seem magical, but it is really just a shortcut for multiplying both sides of the equation by each denominator:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{x-1}{2} & =\frac{2x-1}{5} \\ 2\cdot \frac{x-1}{2} & =2\cdot \frac{2x-1}{5} \\ \cancel{2}\cdot \frac{x-1}{\cancel{2}} & =2\cdot \frac{2x-1}{5} \\ x-1 & =2\cdot \frac{2x-1}{5} \\ (x-1)\cdot 5 & =2\cdot \frac{2x-1}{5}\cdot 5 \\ (x-1)\cdot 5 & =2\cdot \frac{2x-1}{\cancel{5}}\cdot \cancel{5} \\ (x-1)\cdot (5) & =(2)\cdot (2x-1)\end{aligned}
$$

tutorials.name: Cross-Multiplying with a Negative Sign
tutorials.problem:
Consider the following equation:

$$
\dfrac{x+1}{2} = -\dfrac{x}{3}
$$

Even though one of the fractions is negative, we can still use cross-multiplication. All we have to do is transfer the negative into the numerator of the fraction, and proceed with cross-multiplication:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{x+1}{2} & =-\frac{x}{3} \\ \frac{x+1}{2} & =\frac{-x}{3} \\ (x+1)\cdot 3 & =2\cdot (-x)\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we proceed as usual to solve the equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}(x+1)\cdot 3 & =2\cdot (-x) \\ 3x+3 & =-2x \\ 3x+3-3x & =-2x-3x \\ 3 & =-5x \\ \frac{3}{-5} & =\frac{-5x}{-5} \\ -\frac{3}{5} & =x\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $x = -\dfrac{3}{5}.$
